body:
Gandhi's Early Life in Gujarat

Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869 at Porbandar, a princely state in the Kathiawar region of present-day Gujarat. His father, Karamchand Gandhi, also known as Kaba Gandhi, served as the Diwan of Porbandar. His mother was Putlibai.

Gandhi spent his earliest childhood in Porbandar. In November 1876, when he was 7 years old, his family moved to Rajkot. He received much of his early education there. Stories associated with Shravan's devotion to his parents and King Harishchandra's commitment to truth influenced his moral outlook.

Porbandar and Rajkot therefore have distinct places in Gandhi's life: Porbandar was his birthplace, while Rajkot was an important centre of his childhood and education.

From Legal Training to Public Leadership

Gandhi went to England in 1888 to study law. In 1893, he travelled to South Africa, where he confronted racial discrimination against Indians and developed methods of organized nonviolent resistance.

During the South African struggle, Gandhi developed the idea of satyagraha, commonly understood as holding firmly to truth. A satyagrahi resists injustice through nonviolence, self-discipline and a willingness to suffer rather than inflict suffering on an opponent.

Satyagraha

Satyagraha is a method of active, nonviolent resistance to injustice based on truth and moral conviction. It is not passive acceptance of an unjust order.

Gandhi returned to India from South Africa on 9 January 1915. He initially travelled to understand Indian conditions before organizing major local struggles.

Gujarat as a Centre of Gandhian Activity

Gujarat provided Gandhi with an important base for both public service and political action. Ahmedabad became the location of his ashrams and the textile workers' struggle of 1918. Kheda became the setting of a peasant satyagraha in the same year. In 1930, Gandhi began the Salt March from Sabarmati Ashram and ended it at Dandi on the Gujarat coast.

These movements connected national freedom with everyday problems such as wages, agricultural taxation and the price of an essential commodity.

Prelims focus

  • Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869 at Porbandar.
  • His family moved to Rajkot in November 1876.
  • He went to England to study law in 1888.
  • He travelled to South Africa in 1893 and returned to India on 9 January 1915.
  • Satyagraha means active resistance grounded in truth and nonviolence.
  • Trap: Gandhi's birthplace was Porbandar, not Rajkot or Ahmedabad.

[Sources: Gandhi Heritage Portal, “Kirti Mandir, Porbandar” and “Kaba Gandhi No Delo, Rajkot”; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, “Nationalism in India”, pp. 54–55; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, “The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947”, pp. 115–116, 2020–21 printing. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

title: Mahatma Gandhi: From Porbandar and Rajkot to the National Movement

body:
The First Ashram in India

After returning to India, Gandhi established his first Indian ashram at Kochrab, Ahmedabad, on 25 May 1915. It was known as the Satyagraha Ashram and initially operated from a bungalow made available by Jivanlal Desai.

An ashram was more than a residential centre. Its members practised truth, nonviolence, collective labour, simplicity and service. They also undertook education, sanitation and hand-weaving.

The admission of a Dalit family to the Kochrab Ashram demonstrated Gandhi's opposition to untouchability. The decision encountered social resistance, but Gandhi insisted that caste exclusion should have no place in the ashram community.

The Shift to Sabarmati

The ashram moved from Kochrab to a new site near the Sabarmati River on 17 June 1917. The plague outbreak near Kochrab was an important reason for seeking a safer location.

Sabarmati Ashram became Gandhi's home and a major centre of public activity from 1917 to 1930. It served as a place for training volunteers, practising constructive work and preparing nonviolent campaigns. The Dandi Salt March began from this ashram in 1930.

Distinguish the 2 ashrams

Kochrab: Gandhi's first Indian ashram, established in Ahmedabad in 1915.
Sabarmati: The ashram to which the community moved in 1917 and from which the Salt March began in 1930.

Meaning of Constructive Work

Constructive work referred to activities intended to improve society while strengthening people's ability to govern themselves. For Gandhi, political independence and social reform were closely connected.

  • Khadi and hand-spinning: Encouraging locally produced cloth and productive work as alternatives to dependence on imported textiles.
  • Village industries: Supporting employment and economic self-reliance.
  • Removal of untouchability: Challenging caste-based exclusion in public and community life.
  • Sanitation and manual work: Promoting cleanliness and the dignity of labour.
  • Communal harmony: Encouraging cooperation among religious communities.
  • National education: Developing educational institutions connected with Indian languages, society and public service.

These activities were not substitutes for the freedom struggle. They were intended to strengthen communities and sustain public participation between major campaigns.

Gujarat Vidyapith

Gandhi founded Gujarat Vidyapith in Ahmedabad on 18 October 1920, during the Non-Cooperation Movement. Its purpose was to promote national education outside dependence on the colonial education system.

Gujarat Vidyapith shows how constructive work could take an institutional form: students were to receive an education connected with service, self-reliance and national development.

Prelims focus

  • 25 May 1915: Kochrab Satyagraha Ashram established in Ahmedabad.
  • 17 June 1917: Ashram shifted from Kochrab to Sabarmati.
  • Sabarmati Ashram was Gandhi's principal base from 1917 to 1930.
  • 18 October 1920: Gujarat Vidyapith established in Ahmedabad.
  • Khadi, village industries, sanitation, social equality and national education were important areas of constructive work.
  • Trap: The ashram founded in 1915 was at Kochrab; Sabarmati became its location in 1917.

[Sources: Gandhi Heritage Portal, “Kochrab Ashram, Ahmedabad”, sections “The Beginning” and “A Challenge”; Gandhi Heritage Portal, “Sabarmati Ashram, Ahmedabad”, sections “Background” and “The Beginning”; Gujarat Vidyapith, “Journey: 1920–1930”, entry for 18 October 1920. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Gandhi’s community activities connect to self-reliance, social reform and national education, illustrated by Gujarat Vidyapith.
pictures.caption: Constructive work connected social reform, self-reliance and national education.

title: Kochrab and Sabarmati Ashrams: Institutions and Constructive Work

body:
Why the Dispute Began

Ahmedabad was an important centre of cotton textile production. During a plague outbreak, mill owners had paid workers an additional amount, commonly called the plague bonus, to help retain labour.

When employers decided to withdraw this bonus, workers faced difficulties because the cost of living remained high. The dispute therefore concerned wages and working conditions, not agricultural land revenue or a government tax.

The workers sought a wage increase of 35%, while mill owners were prepared to offer 20%. Gandhi supported the workers' demand after examining the circumstances.

People Associated with the Struggle

Mahatma Gandhi intervened to help organize a nonviolent struggle and seek a settlement.

Anasuya Sarabhai was an important organizer of Ahmedabad textile workers. She worked for their interests and played a significant role in building the city's labour movement.

Ambalal Sarabhai, Anasuya's brother, was a prominent industrialist associated with the mill owners. Their involvement on different sides of the dispute makes it especially important to distinguish their roles.

Strike, Fast and Settlement

The labour dispute developed into a strike and lockout during February and March 1918. Gandhi urged workers to maintain discipline and avoid violence even when facing economic hardship.

On 15 March 1918, Gandhi began a fast connected with the workers' struggle. A settlement was reached on 18 March 1918, and the fast ended.

The settlement provided for the workers to resume employment and for the wage question to be decided through arbitration. The immediate arrangement included a 35% increase on the first day back and 20% on the second day, followed by an increase subject to the arbitrator's decision. Anandshankar Dhruv was associated with the arbitration.

Demand and settlement are different facts

The workers' demand was 35% and the mill owners' offer was 20%. The March settlement used temporary wage arrangements while the final increase was left to arbitration. These figures should not be treated as identical.

Importance of the Movement

The Ahmedabad struggle demonstrated how satyagraha could be applied to a dispute between industrial workers and employers. It emphasized peaceful collective action, negotiation and an effort to secure a just settlement without hostility.

The organization of textile workers also contributed to the later development of the Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association, popularly known as the Majoor Mahajan Sangh, with which Anasuya Sarabhai was closely associated.

Prelims focus

  • 1918: Ahmedabad mill-workers' satyagraha.
  • The immediate grievance involved withdrawal of the plague bonus and rising living costs.
  • Workers demanded 35%; employers offered 20%.
  • Anasuya Sarabhai: Textile workers' organizer.
  • 15–18 March 1918: Gandhi's fast and the resulting settlement.
  • Trap: Ahmedabad was a labour-wage dispute; Kheda was a land-revenue dispute.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, “The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947”, p. 116, 2020–21 printing; M. K. Gandhi, The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, vol. 14, “Speech to Ahmedabad Mill-Hands” and “Ahmedabad Mill-Hands' Strike”, pp. 268–269, 18–19 March 1918; Gandhi Heritage Portal, event chronology for 15–19 March 1918; Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Heritage City, “Majoor Mahajan Sangh”. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Textile workers in period clothing gather peacefully outside an Ahmedabad cotton mill gate in 1918, with brick buildings and chimneys behind them.
pictures.caption: Textile workers in the industrial setting of Ahmedabad in 1918.

pictures.alt: Bonus withdrawal led to a 35% versus 20% wage dispute, Gandhi's nonviolent intervention and fast, and a settlement referring wages to arbitration.
pictures.caption: The wage dispute developed into a nonviolent strike and negotiated settlement.

title: Ahmedabad Mill-Workers' Satyagraha of 1918

body:
Background: Crop Failure and Revenue Demand

The Kheda Satyagraha of 1918 was an important peasant movement in Gujarat. Agricultural distress following poor harvests and an outbreak of plague made it difficult for many cultivators to pay the land revenue demanded by the colonial government.

Land revenue was a tax collected by the government from agricultural land. The peasants were not demanding higher wages or protesting a new police tax. They wanted the government to suspend or relax revenue collection because crop failure had reduced their capacity to pay.

Gandhi explained that the relevant land-revenue rules provided for suspension when the crop was assessed at 4 annas or less on a 16-anna scale. In simple terms, that meant a yield of about one-quarter or less of the normal crop. Peasants claimed that their crops met this condition, while officials disputed their assessment.

Leadership and Organization

Mahatma Gandhi guided the movement, and Vallabhbhai Patel emerged as a major organizer. Patel gave up much of his successful legal practice to work with the peasants.

Gujarat Sabha, a public association with which Gandhi and Patel were connected, supported the peasants' representations to the government. Workers such as Mohanlal Pandya, Shankarlal Parikh and other local volunteers helped investigate grievances and mobilize villages.

Nadiad became an important centre of the movement. The organized satyagraha began in March 1918, following unsuccessful requests to suspend revenue collection.

Method of Protest

Participating peasants pledged not to pay the disputed revenue voluntarily. They agreed to remain nonviolent and accept the possibility of government action against their land or property.

A central feature was solidarity between cultivators who could pay and those who could not. Gandhi argued that if wealthier peasants paid immediately, poorer peasants might feel compelled to borrow money or sell property to meet government demands. Collective nonpayment was intended to protect them.

Outcome and Historical Importance

The movement ended in June 1918 after limited government concessions, particularly affecting poorer cultivators. The peasants' original demands were not fully accepted, so the result should not be described as the complete cancellation of land revenue across Kheda.

Its importance extended beyond the immediate settlement. The movement demonstrated organized, nonviolent resistance to an agricultural grievance and established a lasting working relationship between Gandhi and Vallabhbhai Patel.

Prelims focus

  • 1918: Kheda Satyagraha in Gujarat.
  • Cause: Crop failure, agricultural distress and inability to pay land revenue.
  • Leaders: Mahatma Gandhi and Vallabhbhai Patel.
  • Important centre: Nadiad.
  • Method: Disciplined, collective refusal to pay the disputed revenue voluntarily.
  • Trap: Kheda did not end with a complete, unconditional cancellation of all land revenue.

[Sources: M. K. Gandhi, The Story of My Experiments with Truth, Part V, “The Kheda Satyagraha”; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, “The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947”, pp. 116–117, 2020–21 printing; Press Information Bureau, “Sardar Patel: Organiser par excellence”, section on Kheda, 2016; Gandhi Heritage Portal, event chronology for March–June 1918. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Reduced crops and continued revenue demands led to Kheda’s disputed suspension request, March 1918 nonpayment and limited June concessions.
pictures.caption: The reasoning behind the peasants' demand for suspension of revenue collection.

title: Kheda Satyagraha of 1918: The Peasants' Revenue Struggle
